title: Choosing yarn for a project
subtitle: How to match yarn weight, fibre, and twist to what a project actually needs
excerpt: The yarn you choose determines how the fabric drapes and holds its shape. Yarn weight and fibre type both play a role.
sourceNotes: Edie Eckman, The Crochet Answer Book. Pauline Turner, How to Crochet (HarperCollins).

glossaryTerms.definition: A standardised category indicating the thickness of the yarn strand, from lace (thinnest) to jumbo (thickest). A heavier weight produces larger stitches on a larger hook.
The number of individual twisted strands that make up the yarn. In UK terms, ply corresponds roughly to weight: 4-ply is fingering weight, 8-ply is DK, 10-ply is aran.

content.text: Choosing the right yarn is one of the decisions that most shapes the outcome of a project.
Yarn weight

sets the stitch size and drape. Fibre affects care requirements and stitch definition; the construction (how tightly the strands are twisted) determines whether the yarn splits on the hook. Getting all of these right produces a piece that works well and lasts.
Weight and project type
Lace weight (1-
ply
equivalent): delicate shawls, lace doilies. Very fine hook and careful tension needed.
Fingering or 4-ply: socks, light shawls, baby clothes. Good stitch definition on small hooks.
DK (8-ply): the most versatile weight. Garments, toys, lightweight blankets, dishcloths.
Aran (10-ply): sweaters, accessories, heavier blankets. Fast to work and good for beginners.
Chunky (12-ply) and above: cushions, baskets, bulky scarves. Projects grow quickly but stitch detail is less fine.
Fibre and project needs
Wool: warm, elastic, forgiving to work. Good for garments and items that need drape or stretch. Check care requirements; many wools are hand-wash only.
Cotton: cool, strong, no stretch. Good for dishcloths, market bags, summer tops. Heavier than wool at the same weight.
Acrylic: washes by machine, low cost, and easy to find. Good for toys, baby items, and anything washed often.
Bamboo and linen: smooth, with a slight sheen and good drape. Suit lightweight garments and accessories in warmer climates.
Construction and workability

Tightly-twisted plied yarn splits less on the hook and shows stitch definition clearly. Loosely-spun or singles yarn (a single strand with no plying) can catch on the hook tip and split. Beginners and people who work at speed find tightly-plied yarn easier to handle.
Common problems

items.symptom: The yarn splits constantly on the hook
items.cause: The yarn has a loose twist or is a singles construction that the hook tip easily catches.
items.fix: Switch to a blunter hook tip (Tunisian hooks and some brand-name hooks have a more rounded tip that splits less). Or switch to a tightly-plied yarn of the same weight.

items.symptom: The finished piece looks nothing like the pattern photo
items.cause: The yarn weight or fibre is different from what the pattern uses, which changes drape and stitch definition.
items.fix: Check the pattern's stated yarn. If the substitution is significantly different in weight, work a gauge swatch first and expect that the finished proportions may differ.

content.text: What to try next
Read the ball band before buying. It is the fastest way to check whether a yarn suits the project. See the ball band guide for how to extract the key details.
